title: Solving quadratic equations by factorising
subtitle: Factorise a quadratic, use the zero product rule and find both solutions.

curriculum.calculator: Non-calculator skill; questions may appear on any paper.

explanation.title: Why factorising helps us solve quadratics
paragraphs: A quadratic equation contains a squared term as its highest power. Examples include x² = 25, x² + 5x = 0, x² + 7x + 10 = 0 and x² − 36 = 0.
A linear equation normally has one solution, but a quadratic equation can have two. For example, both x = 5 and x = −5 satisfy x² = 25 because 5² = 25 and (−5)² = 25.
The key idea is the zero product rule: if two factors multiply to give 0, at least one of the factors must equal 0.
For example, if (x + 2)(x + 5) = 0, then x + 2 = 0 or x + 5 = 0. This gives x = −2 or x = −5.
Factorising turns one quadratic equation into two smaller linear equations. Two brackets give two equations and usually two solutions.
To factorise x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to give c and add to give b. For x² + 7x + 10, the numbers are 2 and 5, so x² + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5).
Signs matter. For x² − x − 12, the numbers are 3 and −4 because 3 × (−4) = −12 and 3 + (−4) = −1. Therefore x² − x − 12 = (x + 3)(x − 4).
If there is no constant term, factor out x. For x² + 5x = 0, write x(x + 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = −5. Do not divide by x because that loses the solution x = 0.
For a difference of two squares, use a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Therefore x² − 36 = (x + 6)(x − 6), so x = −6 or x = 6.
Factorising is not the final answer when the question says solve. Always set each factor equal to 0 and finish both linear equations.
key_points: Rearrange the equation so one side equals 0 before factorising.
Find two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.
The solution has the opposite sign to the number inside its bracket.
Give both solutions unless a context makes one impossible.
Never divide by x when x could equal 0.

steps.title: Make the equation equal 0
steps.text: Move every term to one side. The zero product rule only works when the product equals 0.

steps.title: Factorise the quadratic
steps.text: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

steps.title: Set each factor equal to 0
steps.text: Turn the two brackets into two separate linear equations.

steps.title: Solve both equations
steps.text: Write both values of x. Remember that x + a = 0 gives x = −a.

steps.title: Check the solutions
steps.text: Substitute each value into the original equation. In a context question, reject any value that is impossible.

interactive.title: Solve x² + 3x = 10
interactive.intro: Rearrange the equation, choose the correct factor pair, form the brackets and solve both linear equations. After the walkthrough, practise recognising factor pairs in the Factor Pair Sprint.

worked_examples.title: Solve x² + 3x = 10
steps: The equation does not equal 0, so subtract 10 from both sides: x² + 3x − 10 = 0.
Find two numbers that multiply to −10 and add to 3: 5 and −2.
Set each factor equal to 0: x + 5 = 0 or x − 2 = 0.
Solve both equations: x = −5 or x = 2.
Check both values in the original equation.

worked_examples.title: Solve x² + 7x = 0
steps: Both terms contain x, so factor out the common factor: x(x + 7) = 0.
Use the zero product rule: x = 0 or x + 7 = 0.
Do not divide by x because that would remove the solution x = 0.

worked_examples.title: Solve x² − 36 = 0
steps: Recognise a difference of two squares: x² − 6².
Set each factor equal to 0 and solve both equations.

question_bank.title: Practise solving quadratic equations
question_bank.intro: Start with equations such as x² = 49, then practise factorising, rearranging to equal 0, taking out a common factor, spotting errors and solving GCSE-style context questions. The practice continues with new questions and becomes more varied as the student progresses.
